title: Quantitative Trading
answer: Market microstructure, factor models, execution learning, statistical arbitrage and regime shifts.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: High-Frequency Market Microstructure
children.blurb: High-frequency market microstructure is the study of how trades actually happen at the finest timescales, from the arrival of an order to its execution or cancellation.

children.name: Non-Linear Factor Models
children.blurb: Non-linear factor models extend the linear factor framework by allowing a factor's effect on returns to depend on other factors, on the level of the factor itself, or on the market regime.

children.name: Learning Trade Execution
children.blurb: Learning trade execution is the use of machine learning to decide how, when, and where to place orders in financial markets.

children.name: Statistical Arbitrage
children.blurb: Statistical arbitrage is a quantitative trading approach that looks for relative value between related securities, often using statistical models to identify temporary mispricings.

children.name: Detecting Market Regime Shifts
children.blurb: Detecting market regime shifts is the practice of identifying when the statistical character of a market changes, for example from calm and trending to volatile and mean reverting, or from broad correlation to dispersion.

sections.body: Quantitative trading uses computers to find and act on statistical patterns in financial markets. In this field, artificial intelligence is mostly applied to prediction and control problems: forecasting short term price moves, estimating how much a trade will cost, and deciding when and how to send orders. High frequency market microstructure work uses machine learning to model the order book, the queue of buy and sell interest at each price. Factor models try to explain returns using many inputs at once, and newer non linear versions let neural networks find interactions that linear regressions miss. Execution algorithms learn from past fills to reduce market impact, and statistical arbitrage systems scan thousands of instruments for temporary mispricings. Regime detection tries to tell when the market's underlying behaviour has changed, because a model trained in one environment often fails in another.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this field are mature. Execution algorithms that learn from historical fills are widely used and can measurably reduce slippage relative to simple rules. Short horizon prediction in liquid markets is heavily optimised, and the infrastructure around it is fast and reliable. What is not solved is robustness. Most published machine learning results in finance come from backtests, and backtests are easy to overfit because financial data is noisy, non stationary and limited in length. Genuine out of sample performance is hard to verify, and many strategies decay once capital is allocated to them. Regime shifts remain the central unsolved problem: models do not reliably know when their assumptions have stopped holding. There is also a structural limit, in that any profitable pattern attracts competition and tends to disappear, so the field is in constant motion rather than converging on a stable answer.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here form a chain from market mechanics to strategy to risk. High-Frequency Market Microstructure is the foundation, covering how orders, queues and latency shape what any model can actually observe and trade. Non-Linear Factor Models sits one level up, dealing with return prediction across many instruments and the statistical care that requires. Learning Trade Execution is the applied control problem, about how to buy or sell a position without moving the price against yourself. Statistical Arbitrage is where these pieces combine into a strategy that takes offsetting positions in related instruments. Detecting Market Regime Shifts is the check on all of it, because it asks whether the relationships the other pages rely on are still true. A reader new to the area would start with microstructure, then factor models, then execution, then arbitrage, and treat regime detection as the ongoing question that runs across the whole section.
